extracted.intended_audience: improvisors, improv students and teachers (readers of UCB manual)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for performing and teaching long- and short-form comedy improv, especially practices described in the UCB Comedy Improvisation Manual (e.g., finding the game, framing, listening).

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing means letting your scene partner know that you feel that they have said or done something unusual within the context of the base reality. When you frame, you highlight or underline the unusual so that it stands out to your scene partner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use framing to point out the first unusual thing in the scene so the partnership can build the game from it. Techniques include picking at, questioning, treating it as strange, and being skeptical of the oddity. Framing is useful because a scene partner may not realize they've done something unusual; by framing you effectively say, “I agree that what you did is the first unusual thing in the scene. Let’s use that to build the game.” (page 72)

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding the Game (game of the scene)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'game of the scene' is defined specifically (not merely simplified) and the book lays out a detailed plan on how to get there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than searching for the Game in your own head, find it in the scene partner: either the partner will provide the unusual thing or will frame what you said, thereby identifying it as unusual. The manual elaborates on 'game' in a quite specific way and provides steps to reach it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listening as the primary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding the game is always about listening. New improvisers often fail to listen because they are searching so desperately for the Game of the scene in their own head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize listening to what your partner offers instead of pre-planning your own search for the game; listen for signals (unusual items or framing) from partners that indicate the game's entry point. (page 81)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of consistent terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce and use specific terms (e.g., 'framing') so practitioners have a shared vocabulary to teach, learn, and discuss techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having a single term for a practice helps instructors explain and students understand it; the reviewer notes that having the term 'framing' will allow clearer, more succinct explanations and easy referral to the book's chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and concrete examples in teaching materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructional material should lay ideas out very clearly and use lots of examples and small graphics to illustrate points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'patient' presentation (stepwise, example-rich, with visuals) helps improvisors at every level including complete beginners. The reviewer emphasizes clear layout, many examples, and little graphics as hallmarks of useful teaching material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility to all levels (including beginners)
rubrics_metrics.description: Material and explanations should be approachable so that improvisors at every level, even complete beginners, will find them useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book is described as patient and useful to improvisors at every level; design lessons so novices can digest them though full mastery may take time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive but pragmatic (no fluff)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide thorough coverage (the manual is nearly 400 pages) while avoiding unnecessary stories or ideological arguments about why the method is right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on practical instruction and how-to guidance rather than debating theoretical superiority; be comprehensive yet concise — 'no fluff' — so the material is usable rather than argumentative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organized referenceability for teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure material so instructors can direct students to specific chapters or sections for deeper explanation (e.g., 'refer students to chapter 4').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having clearly organized chapters that cover core terms/practices allows teachers to assign or reference specific sections when students have questions, making the manual a practical classroom resource.
